property_summary: For any depositor and any deposit amount, calling Deposit never decreases that depositor's stored balance (i.e., balances[addr] after Deposit is >= balances[addr] before); the mutant removing the overflow check allows wrapping on large deposits so some inputs make the post-deposit balance smaller than before.

For any depositor and deposit amount, after calling Deposit the depositor's recorded balance is never less than it was before (reference enforces no wrapped-around decrease); the mutant removes the overflow check and can make the post-deposit balance smaller for some large amount causing wraparound.

For any two distinct accounts A and B and any deposit amount x, a Deposit by A does not change B's recorded balance (reference preserves balances of other accounts; mutant can cause overflow wrap to alter unrelated mapping slots when msg.sender aliasing or storage collision occurs).

For any depositor and any deposit amount, after Deposit completes the depositor's recorded balance is either increased or unchanged (i.e., not decreased); removing the addition-overflow check allows very large deposits to wrap and make the stored balance smaller, violating this rule.

For any actor and any deposit amount, performing Deposit never makes any account's balances value decrease compared to before for that same account; removing the addition overflow check allows a very large deposit to wrap and produce a smaller stored balance for the depositor, violating this rule.

For any caller and any positive deposit amount, the reference contract always increments the caller's balances[msg.sender] by that amount after Deposit; the mutant instead increments balances[address(0)] and thus for some caller/amount the caller's balance does not increase, violating the rule.

For any caller and deposit amount, the correct contract increments balances(msg.sender) by the sent amount after Deposit; the mutant credits balances(address(0)) instead, so there exist inputs where balances(msg.sender) does not increase while balances(address(0)) does.

For any caller and any deposit amount, after calling Deposit the caller's balances[msg.sender] increases by the deposited amount; the mutant instead credits balances[address(0)] so there exist inputs where the caller's balance does not increase while address(0) does.

For any caller and deposit amount, after Deposit the caller's balances[msg.sender] increases by the deposited amount; the mutant instead credits balances[address(0)] so there exist inputs where the caller's balance does not increase while balances[address(0)] increases.

For every caller and deposit amount, after Deposit the reference increases balances(msg.sender) by the deposited amount; the mutant instead increments balances(address(0)) so there exist inputs where balances(msg.sender) does not increase while balances(address(0)) does.

Invariant: Depositing ETH via Deposit increases the caller's mapping entry by the deposit amount and does not change balances for other addresses; the mutant incorrectly decrements balances[address(0)] on every deposit, violating the invariant when the deposit amount > 0.

For any depositor and any deposit amount > 0, the total sum of all stored balances in the contract (sum over mapping entries readable via public getter for the depositor and address(0)) increases by exactly the deposit amount; the mutant wrongly decreases balances[address(0)] causing the total stored-sum to be less than the deposit for some inputs.

For any depositor address A and any deposit amount v >= 0, after calling Deposit() from A with value v, the reference contract's stored balance at address(0) never decreases (i.e., balances(address(0)) after >= before); the mutant decrements balances(address(0)) by v and thus violates this for some inputs.

For any depositor address A and any deposit amount v (v fits into msg.value), the reference contract preserves the invariant that the sum balances[A] + balances[address(0)] increases by exactly v after Deposit() (i.e., only the caller's balance changes and address(0) is unchanged), whereas the mutant decreases balances[address(0)] by v so the sum fails to increase by v for some inputs.

For any depositor address A and any positive deposit v, after Deposit() the reference contract's balances at address A increases by v while balances at some other arbitrary address K do not decrease; the mutant wrongly decrements balances[address(0)] causing there exist K (e.g., address(0)) for which the mapping decreases.

After any Deposit() call by an EOA through a contract caller, the reference contract always credits balances[msg.sender] (the immediate caller) while the mutant incorrectly credits balances[tx.origin], so there exist inputs (a contract caller and sender) where balances at some key differ.

For any caller that invokes Deposit through a forwarding contract, the reference C always increments balances keyed by the immediate caller (msg.sender); the mutant instead increments balances[tx.origin], so when a contract forwards a deposit the balances at msg.sender and tx.origin can differ and thus the mutant violates the invariant that the forwarder’s balance increases while the ref’s increases at the forwarder.

For any depositor contract D that calls C.Deposit on behalf of an EOA origin, the reference C always increases balances[D] when D forwards ETH (msg.sender used as key); the mutant using tx.origin may instead increase balances[origin] for some inputs, breaking the rule.

For any two distinct addresses sender (EOA) and forwarder (contract) where forwarder calls C.Deposit() while forwarding Ether, the reference contract always increases balances[forwarder] (msg.sender) by the deposited amount; the mutant that uses tx.origin can instead increase balances[sender], violating that rule for some inputs.

For any EOA depositor that sends ETH to C through an intermediate forwarding CONTRACT, the reference contract always increments balances[forwarder] (the immediate caller) by the deposited amount; the mutant that uses tx.origin may instead increment balances[origin], so there exists a forwarding contract and EOA pair where balances[forwarder] != balances[origin] after Deposit, violating the rule.

For any address provided to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that address in its public Log getter (so c.Log() equals the provided address); the mutant that omits the storage assignment fails to update Log for some inputs.

For any address passed to SetLogFile when contract is not yet initialized, the reference C stores that address into its public Log getter (so c.Log() equals the provided address); the mutant that removed the storage assignment leaves Log unchanged for some inputs, so there exist inputs where c.Log() != provided address.

For any address X passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference contract stores X into its public Log getter (so c.Log() == X); the mutant that removed the assignment leaves Log unchanged for some inputs so there exist X where c.Log() != X.

For any non-zero address provided to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference C stores that address in its public Log getter (c.Log()), whereas the mutant that omits the storage assignment leaves c.Log() unchanged for some inputs, so there exists an input address where c.Log() != provided address.

For every address X passed to SetLogFile before initialization, the reference contract stores X into its public Log getter (so c.Log() == X); the mutant that removed the assignment leaves Log unchanged for some inputs, so there exist X where c.Log() != X.

For any address passed to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that exact address in its public Log getter; the mutant instead always stores the zero address, so there exist inputs for which the stored Log differs.

For any address passed to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that exact address in its public Log getter; the mutant always stores address(0) instead, so there exist inputs where the stored Log differs (i.e., address(c.Log()) == passed address holds for all inputs in reference but is false for some inputs in mutant).

For every address supplied to SetLogFile, the reference stores that exact address in its public Log getter (address(c.Log()) == supplied), whereas the mutant always stores address(0) so this equality can fail for some inputs.

For every address supplied to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that exact address in its public Log getter (address(c.Log()) == supplied), whereas the mutant always stores address(0) breaking this equality for some supplied addresses.

For every address passed to SetLogFile, the reference contract stores that exact address in its public Log getter (address(c.Log()) == supplied), while the mutant instead sets Log to address(0) causing that equality to fail for some inputs.

After any successful call to SetLogFile(addr) (when caller is any address and contract not initialized), the reference C always stores Log equal to the provided address; the mutant that sets intitalized=true before assigning Log can cause Log to differ (observable) for some inputs involving a reentrant/malicious callee address.

For any caller and any callee address, after a successful call to SetLogFile(callee) on the reference C the stored Log getter equals the callee address; the mutant that sets intitalized = true before assigning Log can let reentrant/malicious callee alter behavior so the stored Log may not equal the provided address for some inputs.

For any caller and any provided log-address, after SetLogFile(addr) completes on the reference contract C the public Log getter equals the supplied address; the mutant that sets intitalized = true before assigning Log can be broken by a malicious callee that performs a reentrant call during SetLogFile, leaving Log not equal to the supplied address.

For every provided log-address and caller, after calling SetLogFile(addr) on the correct contract C, the stored Log getter equals the provided address; the mutant that sets intitalized=true before assigning Log can be exploited by a reentrant malicious contract so that after SetLogFile completes the stored Log does not equal the provided address.

For any caller and any provided log-address, after calling SetLogFile(addr) on the correct contract C the public Log getter equals the provided address; the mutant that sets intitalized = true before assigning Log can be exploited by a reentrant/malicious log contract which during SetLogFile calls back into C and changes state so that after completion the stored Log no longer equals the originally supplied address.

For any depositor and deposit amount, a successful Deposit call on the correct contract always results in the balances[depositor] being increased by exactly the sent msg.value (so address(c).balance equals sum of balances); the mutant that logs before updating balances can be distinguished when the logger's AddMessage reverts (causing Deposit to revert) or behaves adversarially and thus prevents the balance update — so there exist inputs (a failing logger) that make the mutant fail while the reference still satisfies the rule.

For any depositor and amount, a successful call to Deposit increases both c.balances(depositor) and address(c).balance by exactly the sent amount; the mutant that calls Log.AddMessage before updating balances will revert (breaking success) when the logger reverts, so there exist inputs (a failing logger address and some deposit amount) where the mutant fails but the reference still satisfies the rule.

For any depositor and deposit amount, when the contract's LogFile may revert (adversarial callee), the reference C always increases balances(depositor) and address(c).balance by the sent amount when Deposit returns (i.e., Deposit succeeds), whereas the mutant that calls Log.AddMessage before updating balances may revert (or fail to update balances) for some inputs — so a successful Deposit must imply balances[depositor] == sent amount and address(c).balance == sent amount (the mutant can violate this by reverting before updating balances).

For any depositor and deposit amount where the external LogFile call succeeds or reverts, if Deposit returns successfully then the depositor's balances[depositor] equals the total value received (i.e., their previous balance plus msg.value) — the mutant that logs before updating balances can revert when the logger fails, causing Deposit to fail and thus violating that successful-return implies balance updated property for some logger behaviors.

For any depositor and deposit amount, if Deposit returns successfully then the depositor's recorded balance (balances[depositor]) equals the contract's received value for that depositor (i.e., previous balance + msg.value); the mutant that logs before updating balances can be made to revert/behave so that Deposit may return while balances is not updated for some adversarial logger ordering, violating this rule.

For any caller and any nonzero msg.value, after calling Deposit() the caller's balances[msg.sender] increases by exactly the deposited amount in the reference; the mutant that removed balances increment can leave balances unchanged, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller depositing a positive amount, the reference contract always increases the caller's balances[msg.sender] by the deposited msg.value, whereas the mutant that removed the increment can leave balances unchanged for some deposits.

For any depositor address and nonzero deposit value, after calling Deposit the reference contract's overall contract balance (address(c).balance) increases by the deposited amount and equals the sum of all recorded per-address balances via the public balances getter for that depositor; the mutant (which omits updating balances) can still receive ETH (so address(c).balance increases) but balances[msg.sender] will not reflect the deposit, breaking the equality for some inputs.
